C0.quote: the society needs to apply a rule, or social choice function
C0.note: Binary social choice functions aggregating voters' preferences over two alternatives.

C1.quote: a new geometric characterization of anonymous, strategy-proof scfs
C1.note: Characterisation of rules satisfying anonymity and strategy-proofness; strategy-proofness is treated as a property.

C2.1.value: profile P = (Pv)v∈V of preferences; profiles of preferences
C2.1.quote: based upon the profile P = (Pv )v∈V of preferences expressed

C2.2.quote: Pv = a, b, ab, to mean a ≻ b, b ≻ a, or a ∼ b
C2.2.note: Weak orders over two alternatives, with indifference allowed.

C2.3.quote: for every voter v, for every profile P, and for every weak ordering Qv
C2.3.note: True preference Pv is used to evaluate outcomes, separately from the declared Qv.

C2.4.note: Separate notation: Pv is the held preference and Qv a possible declaration; the text says declarations may be false.

C3.1.quote: this agent can advantageously manipulate P (k + 1, m) by declaring indifference
C3.1.note: The main result characterises strategy-proof rules. Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 are purely combinatorial supporting results with no voter behaviour, so ALL was chosen over SOME.

C4.1.note: No utility, welfare, satisfaction, cost, distortion or intensity notions are used for voters.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' is not used.

C5.1.note: Results concern anonymity and strategy-proofness only.

VOT.quote_behav: this agent can advantageously manipulate P (k + 1, m)
VOT.note: Voters' possible manipulation underlies the strategy-proofness property; no information assumption is stated.

C8.1.quote: non-manipulable, if φ(Pv , P−v ) ≻ φ(Qv , P−v ), for every voter v

C8.2.quote: typical assumptions on the scf φ are anonymity and strategy-proofnes

claims.quote: To ensure a fair consideration of the opinions of all agents

C9.1.note: Motivational claim that anonymity ensures fairness to voters and that strategy-proofness prevents false declarations.

C9.2.note: The fairness claim needs inputs to reflect opinions. The same sentence states that strategy-proofness prevents false declarations, which links inputs to held preferences.

C10.1.note: The paper has no conclusion section.

C2.4.reason: The paper uses separate notation (Pv vs Qv) and says declarations can be strategically false, which is the DIST condition rather than IDU.

C9.2.reason: The assumption linking submitted inputs to held opinions is stated in the same sentence, since strategy-proofness is said to prevent false declarations.
